```{r setup}
library(simCoDaR)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 6, dpi = 120)
```

## Which simCoDaR workflow is this?

| Workflow | Starting point | Output |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **This vignette: hypothetical mineralogy** | User-defined mineral targets, domain weights and spread | Known mineral fractions and ideal theoretical chemistry |
| [Measured-assay vignette](measured-assays.html) | Observed compatible assay parts | New compositional draws from an empirically fitted statistical distribution |

The two workflows answer different questions. **Neither automatically
calibrates a deposit**, and an assay-only statistical fit does not identify
the individual minerals that produced the chemistry.

## 1. Start with a mineral mass mixture

This vignette follows mineral targets through synthetic mineralogy to theoretical
chemistry for iron ore, gold, nickel and manganese. These are new hypothetical
illustrations, using the same public API as the package's two-domain example;
they do not reproduce unavailable historical examples. All target values,
probabilities and spreads are author choices, without deposit calibration.

A **domain** is a label for a mixture distribution. Its target mineral proportions
are distinct from the ideal chemical endmembers represented by the mineral
library. Closed mineral fractions sum to one. Multiplying by 100 gives phase
mass percentages. Atom-count stoichiometry then gives bulk elemental wt% and
oxide equivalents; multiplying element wt% by 10,000 gives ppm by mass.

The wrapper calls its reporting tables `observed`: XRD-style phase mass%,
XRF-style oxide wt% and ICP-style element ppm. They have no diffraction
intensities, instrument response or added measurement noise. Truth/reporting
separation is organizational, and both remain available.

## 2. Inspect the ideal formulas

```{r library}
lib <- mineral_assay_library()
selected <- c("Hematite", "Magnetite", "Goethite", "Quartz", "NativeGold",
              "Pyrite", "Bunsenite", "Lizardite", "Pyrolusite", "Manganite",
              "Rhodochrosite")
formula_table <- tibble::tibble(
  mineral = selected,
  formula_label = purrr::map_chr(lib[selected], function(z) z$formula),
  atoms = purrr::map_chr(lib[selected], function(z)
    paste(names(z$atoms), z$atoms, sep = "=", collapse = ", ")))
knitr::kable(formula_table, row.names = FALSE)
```

Formula strings are labels; explicit positive atom counts control calculation.
Formula mass is the sum of atom counts times the package atomic weights. An
individual element's mass fraction is its atom mass contribution divided by
that formula mass. Fe2/Fe3 and Mn2/Mn3/Mn4 encode valences. A compatible supplied
library needs named formula/atoms entries, supported elements and compatible
oxygen/volatile stoichiometry (or supported oxygen-free native/sulfide formulas).
These examples use only the built-in library. Its source attribution and fixed
constants are recorded in the package's `inst/PROVENANCE.md` and source; these
are sufficient assumptions for the hypothetical arithmetic used here.

## 3. Choose four two-domain targets

```{r targets}
targets <- list(
  iron = rbind(
    rich = c(Hematite = .55, Magnetite = .20, Goethite = .15, Quartz = .10),
    gangue = c(Hematite = .10, Magnetite = .05, Goethite = .05, Quartz = .80)),
  gold = rbind(
    rich = c(NativeGold = 5e-6, Pyrite = .08, Quartz = 1 - .08 - 5e-6),
    gangue = c(NativeGold = .5e-6, Pyrite = .02, Quartz = 1 - .02 - .5e-6)),
  nickel = rbind(
    rich = c(Bunsenite = .02, Lizardite = .58, Quartz = .40),
    gangue = c(Bunsenite = .002, Lizardite = .398, Quartz = .60)),
  manganese = rbind(
    rich = c(Pyrolusite = .45, Manganite = .15, Rhodochrosite = .10, Quartz = .30),
    gangue = c(Pyrolusite = .08, Manganite = .04, Rhodochrosite = .03, Quartz = .85)))
weights <- c(rich = .4, gangue = .6)
spread <- c(rich = .25, gangue = .15)
seeds <- c(iron = 42, gold = 43, nickel = 44, manganese = 45)
stopifnot(all(vapply(targets, function(t) max(abs(rowSums(t) - 1)) <= 1e-10,
                     logical(1))))
for (commodity in names(targets)) {
  cat("\n", commodity, "target fractions\n")
  print(targets[[commodity]], digits = 7)
}
```

The constructor normalizes each target row. Normalized targets are geometric
centers in isometric log-ratio (ILR) coordinates for the untruncated generator,
not guaranteed arithmetic sample means. Weights give independent domain-label
probabilities, so 200 samples need not contain exactly 80 rich samples.
`logratio_sd` is an isotropic normal standard deviation in orthonormal ILR
coordinates on each domain's positive support, rather than percentage error bars.

## 4. Draw mineralogy, convert it, then use the wrapper

```{r direct}
iron_spec <- new_assay_scenario(targets$iron, weights = weights,
                                 logratio_sd = spread)
draw <- simulate_assay_scenario(iron_spec, n = 200, seed = seeds[["iron"]])
assay <- minerals_to_assay(draw$composition, basis = "fraction")
assay_percent <- minerals_to_assay(100 * draw$composition, basis = "percent")
stopifnot(max(abs(as.matrix(assay$elements - assay_percent$elements))) <= 1e-6,
          max(abs(as.matrix(assay$element_ppm - assay_percent$element_ppm))) <= .01,
          max(abs(as.matrix(assay$oxides_reported -
                            assay_percent$oxides_reported))) <= 1e-6)
head(tibble::tibble(sample_id = draw$sample_id, domain = draw$facies,
                Hematite_mass_percent = 100 * draw$composition$Hematite,
                Fe_ppm = assay$element_ppm$Fe), 4)
```

Conversion requires inputs already closed to the declared basis. It does not
silently renormalize rows. The default `closure_tolerance = 1e-6` is in input
basis units: fraction units for `fraction`, mass-percent units for `percent`.
Bulk elements include oxygen and all represented elements; a selected metal
subset should not be closed separately. Oxide wt% is neither metal wt% nor ppm.

```{r wrapper}
iron <- simulate_mineral_assay_scenario(iron_spec, n = 200, seed = seeds[["iron"]])
stopifnot(identical(draw$sample_id, iron$sample_id),
          identical(draw$facies, iron$domains$domain),
          identical(draw$composition, iron$truth$mineral_fraction),
          identical(assay, iron$truth$assay))
names(iron$observed)
names(iron$truth)
iron$metadata[c("units", "calibrated", "measurement_model",
                "truth_equals_ideal_reporting")]
scenarios <- purrr::map(targets, new_assay_scenario, weights = weights,
                         logratio_sd = spread)
results <- c(list(iron = iron), purrr::map2(scenarios[-1], seeds[-1],
  function(scenario, seed) simulate_mineral_assay_scenario(scenario, n = 200, seed = seed)))
```

`sample_id` keys the domain table and rows in all mineral/chemistry tables.
`truth$mineral_fraction` retains fractions, while `truth$assay` includes physical
components, water/volatiles, unreported elements and mass-balance audits.

## 5. Control spread, bounds and absence

Zero spread returns each sampled domain's normalized target. Compare it with the
positive-spread iron draw; finite sample variability is descriptive.

```{r controls}
fixed_spec <- new_assay_scenario(targets$iron, weights = weights, logratio_sd = 0)
fixed <- simulate_assay_scenario(fixed_spec, n = 200, seed = 42)
stopifnot(max(abs(as.matrix(fixed$composition) -
                  targets$iron[fixed$facies, , drop = FALSE])) <= 1e-10)
spread_data <- tibble::tibble(
  sample_id = draw$sample_id,
  domain = factor(draw$facies, levels = c("rich", "gangue")),
  fixed_Hematite_mass_percent = 100 * fixed$composition$Hematite,
  varied_Hematite_mass_percent = 100 * draw$composition$Hematite)
spread_comparison <- dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(spread_data, domain),
  dplyr::across(dplyr::ends_with("mass_percent"), sd, .names = "{.col}_SD"),
  .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(spread_comparison, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
bounded_spec <- new_assay_scenario(targets$iron, weights = weights,
  logratio_sd = spread, composition_bounds = list(Hematite = c(.05, .90)))
bounded <- simulate_assay_scenario(bounded_spec, n = 200, seed = 42,
                                    max_draw_attempts = 1000)
range(bounded$composition$Hematite)
bounded$assumptions$composition_rejection_rate
```

Bounds use fraction units and reject candidates, changing the accepted
distribution. The rejection rate is rejected candidates divided by attempted
candidates. Exhaustion of the finite per-domain rejection-round budget stops
instead of relaxing bounds. No monotonic finite-sample SD claim is needed.

Structural absence requires a zero target and the part name in
`structural_parts`; it remains zero only in domains where its target is zero.
This differs from censored trace values or detection limits. Both gold targets
here are strictly positive, with no structural zeros or censoring.

## 6. Read commodity-specific chemistry

Gold's NativeGold fraction `5e-6` equals **0.0005 mineral mass%** and **5 Au ppm**;
`0.5e-6` equals **0.00005 mass%** and **0.5 Au ppm**. These are target values,
not promised sampled arithmetic means. Gold is supplied explicitly, not inferred
from Pyrite. Au has no reported oxide: `element_ppm$Au` holds ppm and
`unreported_elements$Au` holds elemental wt%. Pyrite remains nonoxide physical
mineral mass, while its Fe receives a reported oxide equivalent.

Bunsenite is the library's ideal NiO (`Ni=1,O=1`). Lizardite has Mg, Si, O and H,
and contains no Ni in this library. Thus this example is an ideal NiO-bearing
mixture, not a calibrated laterite or nickel-bearing serpentine model. Using the
package constants, Ni's fraction in NiO is
`58.6934 / (58.6934 + 15.999) = 0.7858015`: 2 mineral mass% gives about
1.571603 Ni wt%, or 15716.03 Ni ppm. NiO reported wt% equals Bunsenite mass%
here; Ni elemental wt% differs. No nickel sulfide or solid-solution model is implied.

Pyrolusite, Manganite and Rhodochrosite have Mn mass fractions approximately
0.6319363, 0.6246932 and 0.4779463. Encoded valences yield separate MnO2, Mn2O3
and MnO columns. Their sum must not be relabelled as MnO or elemental Mn.
H2O and CO2 equivalents are bookkeeping, not measured loss on ignition.

```{r target-chemistry}
target_assays <- purrr::map(targets, minerals_to_assay)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  domain = rownames(targets$gold),
  NativeGold_mass_percent = format(100 * targets$gold[, "NativeGold"], scientific = TRUE),
  Au_ppm = target_assays$gold$element_ppm$Au,
  Au_unreported_wt_percent = format(target_assays$gold$unreported_elements$Au,
                                   scientific = TRUE)), row.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(max(abs(target_assays$gold$element_ppm$Au - c(5, .5))) <= .01,
          abs(target_assays$nickel$element_ppm$Ni[1] - 15716.03) <= .01,
          max(abs(target_assays$nickel$oxides_reported$NiO -
                    100 * targets$nickel[, "Bunsenite"])) <= 1e-6)
knitr::kable(target_assays$manganese$oxides_reported[c("MnO2", "Mn2O3", "MnO")],
             digits = 4, caption = "Manganese target oxide equivalents (wt%).")
```

Summaries below are arithmetic sample means and SDs, distinct from target centers.
Each table retains its own mineral, element and oxide units; trace gold is
formatted scientifically so rounding does not hide it.

```{r summaries, results='asis'}
primary_mineral <- c(iron = "Hematite", gold = "NativeGold", nickel = "Bunsenite",
                     manganese = "Pyrolusite")
primary_element <- c(iron = "Fe", gold = "Au", nickel = "Ni", manganese = "Mn")
oxide_fields <- list(iron = c("FeO", "Fe2O3"), gold = c("FeO", "SiO2"),
                     nickel = c("NiO", "MgO"), manganese = c("MnO2", "Mn2O3"))
for (commodity in names(results)) {
  x <- results[[commodity]]
  values <- tibble::tibble(sample_id = x$sample_id,
    domain = factor(x$domains$domain, levels = c("rich", "gangue")),
    mineral = x$observed$xrd_phase_percent[[primary_mineral[[commodity]]]],
    element = x$observed$icp_element_ppm[[primary_element[[commodity]]]])
  values <- dplyr::bind_cols(values,
    tibble::as_tibble(x$observed$xrf_oxide_wt_percent[oxide_fields[[commodity]]]))
  tab <- dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(values, domain),
    n = dplyr::n(), mineral_mean = mean(mineral),
    element_mean = mean(element), element_SD = sd(element),
    dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(oxide_fields[[commodity]]), mean), .groups = "drop")
  names(tab)[3:5] <- c(paste0(primary_mineral[[commodity]], "_mean_mass_percent"),
                       paste0(primary_element[[commodity]], "_mean_ppm"),
                       paste0(primary_element[[commodity]], "_SD_ppm"))
  names(tab)[-(1:5)] <- paste0(oxide_fields[[commodity]], "_mean_wt_percent")
  if (commodity == "gold") tab$NativeGold_mean_mass_percent <-
    format(tab$NativeGold_mean_mass_percent, scientific = TRUE, digits = 4)
  cat("\n\n", knitr::kable(tab, format = "html", digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = c("Domain", "n", paste(primary_mineral[[commodity]], "mass%"),
                  paste(primary_element[[commodity]], "ppm"),
                  paste(primary_element[[commodity]], "SD (ppm)"),
                  paste(oxide_fields[[commodity]], "wt%")),
    caption = paste(commodity, "sample means and elemental SD")), "\n\n", sep = "")
}
```

```{r domain-plots, fig.cap='Synthetic marginal elemental densities and individual samples, 200 per commodity. Each panel retains its own ppm scale; jitter changes category position only.'}
plot_data <- dplyr::bind_rows(purrr::imap(results, function(x, commodity_name) {
  tibble::tibble(sample_id = x$sample_id, commodity = commodity_name,
    domain = factor(x$domains$domain, levels = c("rich", "gangue")),
    ppm = x$observed$icp_element_ppm[[primary_element[[commodity_name]]]])
}))
plot_data <- tidyr::pivot_longer(plot_data, ppm, names_to = "unit", values_to = "value")
plot_data$commodity <- factor(plot_data$commodity, levels = names(results),
  labels = c("Iron / Fe (ppm by mass)", "Gold / Au (ppm by mass)",
             "Nickel / Ni (ppm by mass)", "Manganese / Mn (ppm by mass)"))
colors <- c(rich = "#007C91", gangue = "#C75B2A")
raincloud <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_data,
  ggplot2::aes(x = domain, y = value, fill = domain)) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(orientation = "vertical", side = "right",
    normalize = "panels",
    subscale = function(z) ggdist::subscale_thickness(sqrt(z)),
    show_slab = TRUE, show_interval = FALSE,
    show_point = FALSE, trim = TRUE, scale = .5, justification = 0,
    position = ggplot2::position_nudge(x = .12), alpha = .65, slab_colour = NA) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(color = domain), size = .7, alpha = .55,
    position = ggplot2::position_jitter(width = .06, height = 0, seed = 20261014),
    show.legend = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ commodity, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = colors, name = "Domain") +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = colors, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = c(.3, .7))) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Hypothetical domain", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.x = ggplot2::element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
withr::with_preserve_seed(print(raincloud))
```

Half-clouds show smoothed marginal distributions of synthetic samples within each
domain. Density thickness uses a square-root display scale, normalized within
each panel, to keep broad rich-domain Au and Ni clouds visible alongside narrower
gangue clouds. Thickness is not a domain count or an uncertainty interval. Points retain exact ppm values; jitter seed 20261014 moves
only their categorical positions. Separate vertical scales keep trace Au readable.
These marginal distributions do not display pairwise correlations or prove causality.

Deterministic conversion gives straight-line mineral-to-element relationships
when an element has one host (Au in NativeGold, Ni in Bunsenite here). Fe and Mn
have multiple hosts in these mixtures. Closure and domain mixing also shape
correlations; these associations have no causal interpretation.

## 7. Audit mass and iron reporting

Default iron reporting keeps FeO and Fe2O3 separate. On the same fractions,
`total_Fe2O3` replaces them with `Fe2O3_total`; FeO is omitted. Magnetite's Fe(II)
contribution makes the added oxygen equivalent visible, while elemental and
physical mass stay unchanged.

```{r iron-reporting}
total_iron <- minerals_to_assay(draw$composition, iron_reporting = "total_Fe2O3")
stopifnot("Fe2O3_total" %in% names(total_iron$oxides_reported),
          !"FeO" %in% names(total_iron$oxides_reported),
          identical(assay$elements, total_iron$elements),
          identical(assay$oxides_physical, total_iron$oxides_physical))
audit_fields <- c("mineral_mass_wt_pct", "element_mass_wt_pct",
                  "physical_components_wt_pct", "reported_components_wt_pct",
                  "reporting_oxygen_gain_wt_pct")
knitr::kable(rbind(
  separate = assay$mass_balance[1, audit_fields],
  total_Fe2O3 = total_iron$mass_balance[1, audit_fields]), digits = 4,
  caption = "Same first iron sample: mass-balance fields in wt%.")
```

Physical components include oxide-compatible physical oxides, H2O and CO2
equivalents, and nonoxide mineral mass. Reported components use cation oxide
equivalents, water, CO2 and unreported elements. Oxygen gain is the reported
component total minus 100 wt%, not measurement error. Reported oxides are never
renormalized; neither they nor their sum alone need equal 100. Do not close
oxide wt% and elemental ppm together.

```{r invariants}
audit_errors <- dplyr::bind_rows(purrr::imap(results, function(x, commodity) {
  a <- x$truth$assay
  fraction_error <- max(abs(rowSums(x$truth$mineral_fraction) - 1))
  percent_error <- max(abs(rowSums(x$observed$xrd_phase_percent) - 100))
  element_error <- max(abs(a$mass_balance$element_mass_wt_pct -
                            a$mass_balance$mineral_mass_wt_pct))
  physical_error <- max(abs(a$mass_balance$physical_components_wt_pct -
                             a$mass_balance$mineral_mass_wt_pct))
  ppm_error <- max(abs(as.matrix(a$element_ppm - 10000 * a$elements)))
  tables <- c(x$observed, list(x$truth$mineral_fraction),
              a[vapply(a, is.data.frame, logical(1))])
  stopifnot(identical(x$sample_id, x$domains$sample_id),
            all(vapply(tables, function(t) identical(rownames(t), x$sample_id), logical(1))),
            fraction_error <= 1e-10, percent_error <= 1e-8,
            element_error <= 1e-6, physical_error <= 1e-6, ppm_error <= .01,
            identical(x$observed$xrd_phase_percent, 100 * x$truth$mineral_fraction),
            identical(x$observed$xrf_oxide_wt_percent, a$oxides_reported),
            identical(x$observed$icp_element_ppm, a$element_ppm))
  tibble::tibble(commodity = commodity, fraction_closure_error = fraction_error,
             phase_percent_closure_error = percent_error,
             element_mass_error_wt_percent = element_error,
             physical_mass_error_wt_percent = physical_error,
             ppm_factor_error = ppm_error)
}))
audit_display <- dplyr::mutate(audit_errors,
  dplyr::across(-commodity, function(z) format(z, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)))
knitr::kable(audit_display, row.names = FALSE)
```

These are arithmetic invariants, not calibration evidence. Element and physical
mass audits use 1e-6 wt%; fraction closure uses 1e-10. The displayed ppm factor
check allows 0.01 ppm. No random sample mean is asserted equal to its target.

## 8. Reproduce within stated limits

An explicit seed restores caller RNG state on success or error, including when
initially absent; `seed = NULL` consumes the caller's stream. RNG kind is unchanged
and recorded. Matching inputs, R/package versions and RNG kind supports
reproduction; cross-version bitwise identity is not promised.

```{r versions}
list(R = R.version.string, simCoDaR = as.character(packageVersion("simCoDaR")),
     knitr = as.character(packageVersion("knitr")),
     rmarkdown = as.character(packageVersion("rmarkdown")),
     RNGkind = RNGkind(), seeds = seeds, recorded_RNGkind = iron$metadata$RNGkind,
     rng_policy = iron$metadata$rng_policy)
```

Samples are independent conditional on domains, with user-selected uncalibrated
centers/spreads and fixed formulas. There is no measurement uncertainty, censoring,
spatial dependence, recovery or process prediction, or fitted solid solution.
Mineral proportions and ideal chemical reporting are the full scope of this
teaching exercise. This development API may change.

## 9. Moving from assumed domains to empirical distributions

The example above **chooses** domain centres and ILR spread. If you have
measured, compositionally compatible assay columns instead, the separate
[measured-assays vignette](measured-assays.html) demonstrates
`fit_assay_simulator()`, `simulate_assays()` and
`validate_assay_simulator()`. It compares Dirichlet, full-covariance
logistic-normal, fixed-df ILR Student-t and ILR Gaussian-mixture models.

Do not mix their outputs: empirical assay simulations close **selected
assay parts**, whereas this vignette closes **mineral mass fractions**
and applies ideal stoichiometry. There is no implemented bridge that
infers mineral mixtures from an empirical oxide distribution or
simulates XRD/XRF/ICP instrument measurement uncertainty.

Use paired mineralogy and assay observations, compatible reporting bases,
independently assessed mineral chemistry and a separate validation design
before describing any extension as physically calibrated.
